'''''Hypericum undulatum''''', the '''wavy St Johns Wort''', is a herbaceous perennial [[flowering plant]] native to western [[Europe]] and northern [[Africa]]. The [[Botanical name#Components of plant names|specific name]] ''undulatum'' is [[Latin]], meaning "wavy" or "undulated", referring, just as the common name, to the wavy [[leaf margin]]s of the herb. The plant has a [[diploid number]] of 16 or 32.

==Description==

''Hypericum undulatum'' grows {{convert|1.5-12|cm|abbr=on}} tall, typically erect or [[Glossary of botanical terms#decumbent|decumbent]] with a creeping or rooting base. The herb typically has numerous to few narrow stems, each with four wings of tissue that bear black glands. The internodes are longer than the leaves, measuring {{convert|12-65|mm|abbr=on}} long. The sessile leaves have elliptic to narrowly oblong blades measuring {{convert|6-40|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|7-14|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The apex of the leaf is rounded, the margin is [[Glossary of botanical terms#undulate|undulate]], and the base is rounded or [[Cordate (leaf shape)|cordate]]. The leaves have pale undersides and are thinly or thickly [[Glossary of botanical terms#chartaceous|chartaceous]]. The leaves have three, occasionally four, pairs of main lateral [[Leaf venation|vein]]s that arise from the lower quarter of the [[midrib]], as well as a dense tertiary reticulation. Leaves have pale, dense laminar glands and black, close intramarginal glands that are irregular in size.<ref name=Study>{{cite journal |title=Studies in the genus Hypericum L.(Guttiferae) 6. Sections 20. Myriandra to 28. Elodes |last1= Robson |first1= Norman KB |journal= Bulletin of the Natural History Museum, Botany Series |year= 1996 |url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2277196#page/20/mode/1up |page= 78}}</ref>

The [[inflorescence]] of the herb is forty-flowered and arises from one to three nodes, with the ascending or horizontal flowering branches arising from up to six nodes. The lax inflorescence is predominantly cylindrical to [[corymb|subcorymbiform]]. The [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s are {{convert|1-2.5|mm|abbr=on}} long and the lanceolate, entire [[bract]]s and [[bracteole]]s are {{convert|2-4|mm|abbr=on}} long. The star-shaped flowers are {{convert|12-17|mm|abbr=on}} wide and are ellipsoid and obtuse while in bud. The five unequal [[sepal]]s are {{convert|3-5.5|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1-1.8|mm|abbr=on}} wide and are erect in bud and fruit. The sepals each have five to seven veins and six to twenty black punctiform laminar glands. The five bright yellow petals of each flower are tinged with red dorsally and are {{convert|7-10|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|3-4|mm|abbr=on}} wide, typically about twice the length of the sepals. The petals are obovate to oblanceolate and bear few punctiform laminar glands. Flowers have 25 to 40 stamens, the longest of which measure {{convert|5-8|mm|abbr=on}}. The [[Locule|trilocular]], ovoid [[Ovary (botany)|ovaries]] are {{convert|2-3.5|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1-1.5|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The ovoid [[Capsule (fruit)|capsule]]s are {{convert|5-8|mm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|3.5-4|mm|abbr=on}} wide. The cylindrical, yellow-brown seeds are {{convert|0.6-0.8|mm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Study/>

The plant flowers in August and September and seeds germinate in the spring.<ref name=Online/>

==Taxonomy==

''Hypericum undulatum'' occurs in two principal varieties: ''H. undulatum'' var. ''undulatum'' and ''H. undulatum'' var. ''boeticum''. The majority of the species, ''H. undulatum'' var. ''undulatum'', has narrow, undulated leaf margins and reddish flower buds, but a population in [[Sierra Nevada (Spain)|Sierra Nevada]] has flat leaf margins and untinged leaves. This population, named ''H. boeticum'' by [[Pierre Edmond Boissier]], has intermediate characteristics between ''H. undulatum'' and ''[[Hypericum tetrapterum|H. tetrapterum]]''. However, the broad leaves and inflorescence resembling ''H. tetrapterum'' in ''H. boeticum'' is interpreted as parallel development between the two species; the petals and leaves of the species represent a reversion rather than an intermediate condition. The species ''H. boeticum'' is now treated as a variety of ''H. undulatum'' rather than a separate species, but certain scattered populations of true hybrids do occur in the [[Iberian Peninsula]].<ref name=Study/>

==Distribution and habitat==

''Hypericum undulatum'' grows in non-[[calcareous]] fields and marshes, stream banks, fens, and acidic bogs at elevations from sea level to {{convert|2700|m|abbr=on}}. The plant prefers wet areas with lateral water movement.<ref name=Online>{{cite web |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/hypericum-undulatum |title= Hypericum undulatum |website= Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |publisher= Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |access-date= 10 October 2018}}</ref>

''Hypericum undulatum'' occurs in far western Europe and northern Africa. In the United Kingdom, the herb can be found in [[Cornwall]], western [[Devon]], [[Pembrokeshire]], [[Ceredigion]], and [[Merioneth]], and in Ireland it can be found in western [[County Cork]]. In [[continental Europe]] it occurs in [[Brittany]], central and western [[Spain]], and [[Portugal]]. In Africa it occurs in western [[Algeria]], northern [[Morocco]], [[Madeira]], and [[Azores]]. The variety ''boeticum'' occurs only in extreme southern Spain with the variety ''undulatum'' occurring throughout the rest of the distribution.<ref name=Study/>

==Ecology==

''Hypericum undulatum'' typically grows in vegetation dominated by mixtures of ''[[Molinia caerulea]]'', ''[[Juncus acutiflorus]]'', and ''[[Juncus effusus]]''. It also occurs in conjunction with a variety of other herbs, typically including ''[[Angelica sylvestris]]'', ''[[Cirsium palustre]]'', ''[[Filipendula ulmaria]]'', ''[[Galium palustre]]'', ''[[Lotus pedunculatus]]'', ''[[Mentha aquatica]]'', and ''[[Senecio aquaticus]]''.

Population sizes of the herb can vary greatly, increasing especially following reinstatement of grazing or burning in overgrown sites. Decline of ''H. undulatum'' in localities is mostly due to habitat loss, typically resulting from agricultural intensification. Managing populations of the herb in grasslands involves grazing in the summer and occasional burning in the winter.<ref name=Online/>
